annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS

20 November 2026: the Apple TV playing to both HomePods in the living room, and the phone showed the song twice, as two whole cards each with its own Pause, and twice again on Home. The TV already folds them (design/tv-music/): a speaker in the same room playing the same song is counted as playing with it. This is the same question for the phone and the wall.

A: ONE CARD WHILE THEY PLAY TOGETHER

Nothing to set up: two speakers in one room with the same song are one card, named for both, and its Pause and volume work both -- the TV's rule, everywhere. When they play different things, or one stops, they are two cards again.

FOR: no question to answer, and the TV and the phone agree.

AGAINST: the card changes shape when the music starts and stops, and a quiet pair is still two cards.

B: ASKED ONCE, A PAIR FROM THEN ON

The first time two speakers in a room play the same song, the house asks once whether they are one pair, the way a second strip is asked if it is part of the same light. Said yes, they are one card for good, playing or quiet, and music is sent to both. It can be split later from the card.

FOR: the house learns how the household thinks of them, and a quiet pair is one card too.

AGAINST: one more question, asked on a phone at a moment when somebody wanted to listen.

C: ONE CARD LEADS, THE OTHER IS A LINE

The first keeps its card; the other shrinks to a line under it saying it is playing with the first, and comes back as a card when it plays something else.

FOR: both stay visible as the two speakers they are.

AGAINST: still two places to press, and Pause on the card stops only one.

IN EVERY DIRECTION

The card's name no longer sits under the song's title (a fault of the shipped card, fixed whichever wins). Home's On right now says the song once.

DECIDED 20 NOVEMBER 2026

B, with C until it is answered. Until the household says, the first speaker keeps its card and the other is a line under it (C). The house asks once whether they are one pair: One pair makes them one card for good, Two speakers keeps two whole cards.

WHY THIS EXISTS

22 November 2026: two HomePods set up as a stereo pair beside an Apple TV, named Left and Right. The room drew Right as a line under Left and asked whether they were one pair, and the Home row on a computer showed the film twice. But the speakers had already said so: each tells the network the pair it belongs to and which side it is. They cannot be played apart, so Two speakers was never a true answer for them.

A: TOLD BY THE SPEAKERS, ONE CARD FROM THE START

A pair the speakers announce is a pair, with no question: one card from the first moment, playing or quiet, named for both, exactly as a pair the household said yes to. Music sent there goes to the pair. There is nothing to split here; a pair is unmade on the speakers, and the card follows.

FOR: nothing to answer, and nothing on screen that isn't true of the speakers.

AGAINST: the name is the two names joined, which reads a little long for Left and Right.

B: ASKED, WITH THE ANSWER ALREADY GIVEN

The sheet still comes up once, but says what the speakers said and has one button.

AGAINST: a sheet that asks nothing is an interruption at the moment somebody wanted to listen.

C: TOLD, AND NAMED FOR THE ROOM

Like A, but the card is called Living room speakers.

AGAINST: a name the household never gave, and wrong the day a second pair or a speaker of another kind joins the room. The pair's own names are what the household will say in the command box.

DECIDED 22 NOVEMBER 2026

A. Speakers that say they are one pair are one card with no question; the question stays for two speakers that only happen to play the same song.
